title: Safe Mode Boot
summary: Safe mode starts Windows with a minimal driver and service set, and many third party endpoint agents are configured not to load in that state, so rebooting a host into safe mode is an effective way to run without them. An attacker with administrator rights usually prepares the reboot by editing the Boot Configuration Data store, for example by adding a safe mode boot entry, and can then extend the short list of services that start in safe mode through registry values or by registering a component object that loads there. No exploit and no unusual file is strictly required, so the signal is configuration and boot behaviour: changes to the boot configuration, safe mode boot events in the system log, a short boot cycle followed by the same interactive session, and an endpoint agent that stops reporting while the host stays powered on. Legitimate troubleshooting, driver updates, and vendor repair procedures produce the same pattern, so pairing the boot change with what happened on the host afterwards is what separates them.

beginner.definition: Safe mode is a special way to start Windows. It loads only a small set of drivers and services. Many security tools do not start in this mode. An attacker can force a restart into safe mode so that those tools stay off.
beginner.whyItMatters: If the endpoint agent does not start, nobody sees what the attacker does next. The machine still runs, so the user may not notice anything wrong. Safe mode is a normal Windows feature that staff use for repairs. That makes it easy for an attacker to hide behind real work. Watching boot changes and agent gaps is the main defense.
howItWorks: The attacker first gains administrator rights, because the boot settings are protected.
They edit the boot configuration data, which is a set of files that control how Windows starts.
They add an option that starts the system in safe mode on the next restart.
They may also add their own program to the short list of services that safe mode starts.
After the restart, the endpoint protection agent is usually not running at all.
The attacker works on the host, and may remove the boot option later.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel where the night manager always watches the corridor cameras. One evening the manager is called away to a training room. The cameras keep recording, but nobody is watching the screen. A thief walks the corridors in plain sight. In the morning the manager returns and sees nothing unusual in the room. Safe mode is that quiet training room, easy to walk past. The security tool is still installed, but it is not standing at its post.
takeaways: An unexpected safe mode boot on a server is worth investigating the same day.
Track changes to boot configuration on hosts that hold valuable data.
Alert when an endpoint agent stops reporting but the machine stays online.

objectives: Explain what safe mode is and why some security tools do not start in it.
Describe how boot configuration settings can force a host into safe mode.
Identify registry and service changes that let malicious code run in safe mode.
Detect a suspicious safe mode boot using boot records and agent health telemetry.
Explain why routine troubleshooting looks the same and how to tell the two apart.
